implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: derive an absolute deadline from a monotonic clock before the call starts, hand it to the call's wait primitive (blocking with a budget, an async select, or a token the callee can observe), and treat expiry as its own outcome - neither success nor a generic error. Propagate the same deadline downstream with elapsed time deducted instead of computing a fresh full budget at each hop, and make the abandoned work stoppable: if the callee can observe a cancellation signal, send it; if it cannot, ensure the operation is idempotent before any retry. Budgets belong to configuration derived from the dependency's latency distribution, not to a constant copied between call sites. Timeout, retry, bulkhead and circuit breaker must be designed together as a single policy: the timeout caps the per-attempt wait, the retry budget caps total attempts, the bulkhead caps concurrent calls, and the circuit breaker stops all calls when the dependency is clearly down. The composition order matters: CircuitBreaker(Retry(Call)) observes the logical operation; Retry(CircuitBreaker(Call)) observes each physical attempt.
code_sketch:
deadline = monotonic_now() + budget
result = call_with_deadline(peer, payload, deadline)   # blocking, async or token-based
if result is TIMED_OUT:
    cancel(handle)                  # tell the callee to stop, when the protocol allows it
    report(Timeout(peer, budget))   # a definite failure, never a slow success
pitfalls: Leaving the deadline out of the protocol, so the callee cannot know the caller gave up and keeps burning resources on work nobody will read.
Treating expiry as success or as an ordinary error, which makes retries blind and hides a real dependency outage behind a fallback value.
Measuring with a wall clock instead of a monotonic clock, so a clock adjustment silently shortens or extends every budget.
Setting timeouts based on healthy-system p95 latency instead of p99.9 under load, so normal variance triggers spurious failures during peaks.
Adding a timeout without also tuning retries, bulkhead and circuit-breaker thresholds, producing retry amplification that makes the overload worse.
Retrying a non-idempotent operation after a timeout without knowing whether the remote side processed it, risking duplicate side effects (e.g., double payment).

Wrong move: bounding the wait with Thread.join(timeout)/future.get(timeout) and treating expiry as done -> the blocked worker keeps running, holding the connection, lock or row it acquired, and the next timeout fires while the previous abandoned call is still executing -> instead hand the wait primitive an observable cancellation it can act on (interruptible wait, token, socket close), and only accept the leak when the callee provably self-terminates.

Wrong move: re-arming the same per-attempt budget at every retry and every hop -> three 2s attempts plus a downstream chain silently costs 6s+ while the caller's own caller already budgeted 3s, so the timeout 'never fires' at the level that mattered -> instead carry one absolute end-to-end deadline, deduct elapsed time, and skip any retry whose remaining budget cannot finish it.

Wrong move: one timeout value covering pool-queue wait, connect, TLS and read -> a saturated connection pool is logged as a backend timeout, the backend is blamed and tuned, and the real capacity limit stays hidden -> instead time each phase separately (borrow/connect/handshake/read) so a timeout names the phase that actually exceeded its budget.
sources: AWS Well-Architected Framework REL05-BP05 — Set client timeouts: configure both connection and request timeouts explicitly; balance tight enough to release resources against loose enough to avoid retry amplification; use per-dependency values, not a global constant. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/rel_mitigate_interaction_failure_client_timeouts.html
